reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Middleton's Allergy
clinicalPearls: IgE-mediated (type I) reactions to natural rubber latex proteins range from contact urticaria to rhinoconjunctivitis, asthma, and anaphylaxis, and are distinct from irritant or allergic contact dermatitis from rubber-processing chemicals
Healthcare workers, patients with spina bifida or urogenital anomalies, and those with repeated surgical or catheter exposure are at highest risk owing to frequent mucosal and cutaneous contact

Powdered gloves historically amplified sensitisation because latex allergen adsorbed to cornstarch became airborne, so a shift to powder-free low-protein or non-latex gloves has markedly reduced new cases
The latex-fruit syndrome reflects cross-reactivity between latex proteins and plant allergens, so patients may also react to banana, avocado, kiwi, and chestnut
Diagnosis combines a compatible history with skin testing and serum latex-specific IgE; a validated skin test extract may not be uniformly available, making the history and in-vitro testing important
Reactions can occur through skin, mucosal, inhalational, or parenteral routes, and intraoperative anaphylaxis may be the presenting event when latex is contacted internally
Cornerstones of care are strict avoidance, a latex-safe environment for procedures, medical-alert identification, and a self-injectable adrenaline device for those with systemic reactions
Type IV allergic contact dermatitis from rubber accelerators (e.g. thiurams, carbamates) presents as delayed eczema and is confirmed by patch testing, not by IgE tests
reference.pathophysiology: Type I latex allergy results from IgE sensitisation to water-soluble proteins in natural rubber harvested from Hevea brasiliensis. Repeated cutaneous, mucosal, or airborne exposure drives production of latex-specific IgE bound to mast cells and basophils; re-exposure cross-links this IgE and triggers mediator release causing urticaria, bronchospasm, and anaphylaxis. Airborne allergen bound to glove powder facilitates respiratory sensitisation. Structural homology between latex proteins (e.g. hevein-related and profilin allergens) and plant proteins accounts for cross-reactivity in the latex-fruit syndrome. A separate delayed, T-cell-mediated contact dermatitis is caused not by latex protein but by rubber-manufacturing chemicals.
additionalDifferentials: Irritant contact dermatitis from gloves or hand hygiene
Type IV allergic contact dermatitis to rubber accelerator chemicals
Anaphylaxis from perioperative drugs, antiseptics (chlorhexidine), or antibiotics
additionalInvestigations: Skin prick testing with a standardised latex extract where available
Patch testing for suspected delayed contact dermatitis to rubber chemicals
Serum tryptase during a suspected acute systemic reaction
Supervised glove-use or challenge testing in specialist settings when the diagnosis is uncertain
redFlags: Intraoperative or procedural anaphylaxis with hypotension or bronchospasm requiring immediate intramuscular adrenaline and removal of all latex sources
Progressive airway or respiratory symptoms after mucosal or inhalational latex exposure
Systemic reaction in a high-risk patient (spina bifida, multiple surgeries) not previously identified as latex-allergic
Recurrent reactions despite avoidance suggesting unrecognised hidden latex exposure
reference.prognosis: With reliable avoidance and a latex-safe healthcare environment, most patients avoid further reactions and occupational sensitisation often improves after exposure ceases. Unrecognised sensitisation, however, can lead to severe or fatal perioperative anaphylaxis.
pitfalls: Confusing delayed contact dermatitis from rubber chemicals with true IgE-mediated latex allergy
Failing to arrange a latex-safe environment for surgery or dental and radiological procedures
Overlooking cross-reactive foods in the latex-fruit syndrome
Not counselling the patient to carry medical-alert identification and an adrenaline device
management: The cornerstone is strict avoidance of natural rubber latex within a latex-safe environment, substituting powder-free non-latex (nitrile or vinyl) gloves and equipment
Equip patients for anaphylaxis with an adrenaline auto-injector plus antihistamine and provide a written emergency action plan
Ensure a latex-free perioperative pathway, scheduling affected patients first on the list and flagging the allergy prominently to prevent intraoperative anaphylaxis
Counsel on latex-fruit cross-reactivity, advising caution with banana, avocado, kiwi, and chestnut
Reduce occupational exposure through powder-free low-protein or non-latex gloves for at-risk healthcare workers
Provide a medical-alert identifier and ensure the allergy is documented across all care settings
Refer to allergy and immunology for confirmatory latex-specific IgE and skin testing and ongoing management
